hook: Three levers change model behavior: what you SAY, what it KNOWS, and what it IS. **Choosing wrong wastes weeks — this reel is the decision framework architects actually use.**

scenes.title: Prompt vs RAG vs fine-tune: the three-question decision
scenes.sub: Answer in order — most projects never need the third lever
scenes.narration: The three levers operate at different layers. PROMPTING changes behavior through instructions — cheapest, instant, reversible: new skill formats, tone, output schemas (GA-03/GA-04) — it cannot add knowledge the model doesn't have, and every instruction competes for the same context window (AG-13). RAG changes knowledge through retrieval — inject current, private, citable facts at query time (GA-09/GA-10) — it updates instantly when documents change, but facts ride along every call and consume context. FINE-TUNING changes the model's WEIGHTS — permanent behavior and style baked in, no per-call cost, but it needs hundreds of curated examples, a training pipeline, and every update means retraining. The decision, in order: FIRST ask 'is the knowledge current/private/changing?' → RAG. 'Does the behavior fail even with good prompts and retrieved facts?' → fine-tune. Everything else → prompt. A golden rule from the field: RAG and fine-tuning are complements, not rivals — fine-tune STYLE and FORMAT, RAG the FACTS.

scenes.title: The decision flow, as a function
scenes.body:
def choose_lever(problem) -> str:
    # Q1 · knowledge — current, private, or frequently changing?
    if problem.knowledge_is_private_or_changing:
        return "RAG"        # GA-09/GA-10 — facts injected at query time

    # Q2 · behavior — does it still fail with a great prompt
    #        AND the facts in context?
    if fails_despite_prompt_and_facts(problem):
        if problem.style_or_format_issue:
            return "FINE-TUNE"     # teach the SHAPE it can't follow
        return "prompt harder"     # GA-03 — the lever is underused

    # Q3 · always true, whatever else you chose:
    return "prompt (base) + RAG (facts)"

# Field rules:
#  • Default stack: good prompt + RAG. Fine-tune LAST.
#  • Facts change? Fine-tune can't help — weights freeze at training.
#  • Fine-tune style, RAG facts — complements, not rivals.
annot: Q1 before Q2: adding knowledge is RAG's job — no amount of weight-tuning makes a model know this morning's prices
Fine-tune only after prompt+RAG demonstrably fail — otherwise you're paying to fix what wasn't broken
The default stack line is the answer you'll give in 80% of architecture reviews

scenes.title: SFT, LoRA, PEFT: what fine-tuning actually costs
scenes.sub: You are not retraining GPT — you're steering it with curated examples
scenes.narration: FINE-TUNING means continued training on task-specific examples so the model internalizes behavior — hundreds to thousands of curated input/output pairs, not millions of documents. SFT — supervised fine-tuning — is the base case: show the model prompt + ideal response pairs, adjust weights to raise the probability of those responses — quality beats quantity — 500 excellent examples outperform 5,000 noisy ones, and DATA CURATION is 80% of the project: every mislabeled example teaches the wrong lesson permanently. The engineering breakthrough that made fine-tuning cheap is LoRA — low-rank adaptation: freeze the base model's billions of weights and train tiny adapter matrices — the adapter might be 0.1% of the model's size, trainable on one GPU, swappable at runtime — one base model, many task adapters, selected per request. PEFT is the umbrella — parameter-efficient fine-tuning — LoRA plus siblings (prefix tuning, adapters). The honest trade-offs: training needs GPUs and an eval harness (GA-20) to prove it worked; a fine-tuned model can FORGET base skills; and you now own model versions — the drift and deployment discipline of GA-26 applies to you too.

scenes.title: LoRA fine-tune with a few lines
scenes.body:
from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers import (AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer)
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model
from trl import SFTTrainer

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B")
model = get_peft_model(model, LoraConfig(
    r=16,                 # rank — adapter size; bigger = more capacity
    lora_alpha=32,        # scaling — how hard adapters steer output
    target_modules=["q_proj", "v_proj"],   # attention layers to adapt
))

# 1,000 rows: {prompt, ideal_response} pairs — CURATED.
dataset = load_dataset("json", data_files="support-tone.jsonl")

SFTTrainer(model=model, train_dataset=dataset["train"],
           max_seq_length=2048).train()     # ≈ one GPU, hours not weeks

model.save_pretrained("adapters/support-tone-v3")
# Base model untouched — adapters ship separately (MBs, not GBs)
# and hot-swap per request: same weights, different behavior.
annot: r=16 is the steering wheel — tiny matrices (0.1% of weights) changing behavior dramatically
The dataset line is the real work — curation is 80% of a fine-tune project; garbage teaches garbage
Adapters hot-swap — one base model serves many behaviors, chosen per request at runtime

scenes.title: Distillation & small models: teacher knowledge, student price
scenes.sub: Why the smartest move in GenAI economics is often a smaller model
scenes.narration: DISTILLATION transfers capability from a large TEACHER to a smaller STUDENT: run the teacher on many examples, keep its outputs (or its probability distributions), and train the student to match — the student learns the teacher's reasoning style at a fraction of the parameter count. The economics (GA-25, GA-30) drive everything here: a distilled 8B model served locally can cost 100x less per token than a frontier API model — for the 80% of tasks that are classification, extraction, routing, and formatting, a small model is not a compromise, it's the RIGHT TOOL. Routing architectures exploit this: a cheap classifier decides which queries need the frontier model and which the local one handles — GA-25's cost-model optimizer made structural. The trade-offs are real: students inherit the teacher's blind spots, distilled reasoning chains can be shallow — 'the student copies the answer's shape, not always its depth' — and eval discipline (GA-20) decides whether the student is good ENOUGH per task class. Architect's rule: benchmark a 7-8B open model on YOUR tasks before reaching for the frontier API — you'd be surprised how often it's enough.

scenes.title: Distillation + routing — the economics combo
scenes.body:
# STEP 1 · distill: teacher answers, student learns
#   teacher = frontier API model on 10k unlabeled tasks
#   student  = Llama-3-8B trained on those outputs (SFT, like above)
#   eval gate: student must match teacher ≥ 92% on golden set
#              before it earns traffic (GA-20)

# STEP 2 · route: frontier model only where it earns its price
async def answer(query: str):
    needs_frontier = await router_classify(query)   # cheap, local, ms

    if needs_frontier:                       # ~15% of traffic
        return await frontier_api(query)     # hard reasoning

    return await local_model(query)          # ~85% — 100x cheaper

# Measured outcome (support-triage example):
#   cost/task:  $0.046 → $0.011   (≈76% saving)
#   quality:    task-success 94.1% → 93.4%  (within SLO)
# The 0.7 point you traded was priced into the model.
annot: The eval GATE before traffic — distillation without measurement is hope, not engineering
Routing classifier is itself a small model — the cheap brain decides when to hire the expensive one
Quality drop within SLO at 4x saving — GA-30's triangle: you optimized cost, budgeted accuracy, consciously

scenes.title: Local & open models: Ollama, vLLM, and when your laptop is enough
scenes.sub: Open weights change the build-vs-buy math — and the privacy math
scenes.narration: OPEN-WEIGHT models — Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Phi — let you run capable models on YOUR hardware, and two tools define the practice. OLLAMA is the developer path: one command pulls and serves a model locally — 'ollama run llama3.1' — an OpenAI-compatible endpoint appears on localhost, so EVERYTHING from GA-03 onward — the SDK calls, the prompt patterns, structured output — works unchanged against your laptop; it's the default for prototyping, offline work, and privacy-sensitive experiments. VLLM is the production path: a serving engine built around PAGED ATTENTION — it batches many requests against one model copy with far better GPU utilization — when you self-host at scale, throughput per GPU is the entire economics, and vLLM's continuous batching is the industry answer. The architect's 'when local' checklist: data cannot leave your boundary (health, legal, defense) — local wins outright; predictable high volume — capex + ops can beat per-token pricing past a threshold; regulatory residency — GA-29's private endpoints vs self-host is a real comparison. When NOT: you need frontier reasoning that open models haven't matched yet — check benchmarks on YOUR eval set, not vibes, because the gap closes quarterly.

scenes.title: One API, three backends — prompt once, run anywhere
scenes.body:
from openai import OpenAI

# The SAME client code against three backends — the lever
# is the base_url, nothing else. This is why the OpenAI
# API shape became the industry's universal socket.

backends = {
    # 1 · local laptop (Ollama)
    "local":   OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1",
                      api_key="ollama"),
    # 2 · self-hosted fleet (vLLM, OpenAI-compatible)
    "selfhost": OpenAI(base_url="https://llm.internal.example.com/v1",
                       api_key=service_token),
    # 3 · frontier API
    "frontier": OpenAI(api_key=os.environ["OPENAI_KEY"]),
}

resp = backends["local"].chat.completions.create(
    model="llama3.1",                     # or "my-gpt4o" (GA-29)
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],
)
# Swap backends per tenant, per task class, per cost curve —
# GA-30's cost model and AG-25's compliance matrix both fit here.
annot: localhost:11434 is Ollama's OpenAI-compatible port — zero SDK changes to go offline
vLLM speaks the same protocol — dev on Ollama, prod on vLLM, same code
Backend selection becomes CONFIGURATION — the AG-25 agent-definition pattern applied to model routing

recap: Three levers: prompt (behavior, free), RAG (facts, instant updates), fine-tune (weights, permanent) — decide in that order; default stack is prompt + RAG
SFT teaches with curated examples (quality over quantity); LoRA/PEFT trains tiny adapters — 0.1% of weights, one GPU, hot-swappable per request
Distillation moves a teacher's capability into a cheap student; pair it with routing and the frontier model only sees the traffic that pays for it
Open weights + Ollama (dev) / vLLM (prod, paged attention) give you an OpenAI-compatible socket you own — swap backends via base_url alone

quiz.q: A customer-support bot gives structurally wrong answers despite good prompts and correct retrieved documents — the right FORMAT, wrong STYLE/behavior. Best lever?
opts: Add more documents to the vector store
Fine-tune on curated examples of ideal responses — the behavior lives in the weights, not the facts
Switch to a bigger frontier model
quiz.why: Facts are already right (documents retrieved), instructions already good (prompts tuned) — what remains is behavior the model can't reliably follow. That's exactly what SFT/LoRA fixes: bake the style and format into the weights.

quiz.q: Why can't fine-tuning keep a model current on facts that change daily?
opts: Fine-tuning is too expensive to run daily
Weights freeze at training time — a fact learned in fine-tuning is frozen in the weights, while RAG injects fresh facts at every query
Models forget how to do math if fine-tuned too often
It can — you just need more GPUs
quiz.why: The knowledge-lever distinction: RAG reads current documents at query time (update the store, everything is fresh); fine-tune writes knowledge into weights at train time (fresh only until tomorrow's data arrives). Changing facts → RAG, always.

quiz.q: Your evals show an 8B open model matches the frontier API at 92% task-success on your golden set, comfortably above SLO. Architecturally, what does that unlock?
opts: Nothing — bigger models are always safer choices
A routing architecture: the cheap local model takes most traffic (or all of it), the frontier model only gets the hard remainder — roughly 4-100x cost reduction with quality inside SLO
You must fine-tune the 8B model to close the last 8%
You should switch entirely to the frontier model for reliability
quiz.why: Within-SLO is within-SLO — GA-30's cost triangle says optimize cost and consciously budget the quality margin. Routing (or full local deployment via vLLM) converts the eval result directly into unit economics.

code.title: The lever ladder
code.body:

prompt         behavior      ~0           instant       per call
RAG            knowledge     retrieval    instant       update docs
fine-tune      weights       $ + GPUs     retrain       per release

def choose(p):
    if p.knowledge_is_private_or_changing: return "RAG"
    if fails_despite_prompt_and_facts(p):
        return "FINE-TUNE (LoRA) on curated examples"
    return "prompt + RAG  ← 80% of production answers
annot: The table is the whole reel — everything else is mechanics and judgment calls
Reversibility column is underrated: prompts and RAG roll back in minutes; weights need a retrain or adapter swap
'80%' is experience, not law — but default to the cheap levers and earn the expensive one

notes:
# RAG vs Fine-tune vs Prompt — GA notes

## The framework
1. Knowledge current/private/changing? → **RAG** (GA-09/GA-10).
2. Behavior still failing with good prompt + facts? → **fine-tune**.
3. Otherwise → **prompt harder** — the underused lever.
Golden rule: fine-tune style/format, RAG facts. Complements.

## Fine-tuning mechanics
- SFT on hundreds–thousands of CURATED pairs; data curation = 80% of the project.
- LoRA/PEFT: freeze base, train tiny adapters (r=16 typical). MBs, one GPU, hot-swap per request.
- Risks: catastrophic forgetting, you now own versions/deployment (GA-26), needs eval harness (GA-20).

## Distillation
Teacher outputs → student training data. Gate student on golden set before traffic. Pair with routing: cheap classifier sends ~15% to frontier.

## Local & open
- Ollama: dev/prototype, OpenAI-compatible on localhost:11434.
- vLLM: production serving, paged attention + continuous batching → throughput per GPU.
- When local: data-boundary rules, predictable volume capex, residency.
- When not: frontier-reasoning gap — measure on YOUR evals; the gap closes quarterly.
